title: EgyptAir Flight 990
one_line: A Boeing 767 dived, briefly climbed, then struck the Atlantic, killing all 217 aboard.
status_why: U.S. investigators blamed the relief first officer’s control movements; Egyptian investigators disputed that conclusion and sought further mechanical investigation.

aircraft.livery_notes: Photographed 20 October 1999: white fuselage and tail; broad red window stripe with a narrower gold/tan stripe below; red English and Arabic titles; red/gold tail bands and circular Horus emblem; white engine nacelles. No winglets. Source s12 is eleven days before the accident; same-day livery was not independently verified.

site.description: Eastern seabed debris-field center, 40°20′51″N 69°45′24″W, not a measured water-entry coordinate. The smaller western field lies about 366 m away. Wreckage was recovered in approximately 230 ft of water, converted and rounded to about 70 m. elev_ft=0 denotes the sea surface, not seabed. NTSB printed pp. 7, 34.

events.title: Ready at runway 22R
events.detail: The crew reported holding short and ready for takeoff.
events.caption: The crew reported ready for takeoff, waiting before the runway.

events.title: Takeoff clearance
events.detail: JFK tower cleared the aircraft to take off from runway 22R.
events.caption: The tower cleared the aircraft to take off from runway 22R.

events.title: Airborne recorder signal
events.detail: The air/ground discrete changed from Ground to Air. This is a recorded system transition, not an exact surveyed runway position.
events.caption: The aircraft’s ground sensor switched to airborne, marking takeoff.

events.title: Climb to flight level 230
events.detail: Departure control cleared a climb to FL230 and transfer to New York Center.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft to climb and handed it over to New York Center.

events.title: Direct DOVEY and further climb
events.detail: The aircraft was cleared direct to DOVEY intersection and to FL330.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft toward the DOVEY navigation point and allowed a further climb.

events.title: First officer change
events.detail: Door and seat sounds, with conversation over the next minute, indicated that the relief first officer took the right seat. The exact instant of the seat transfer is not established.
events.locator: s1 p.3; event time is start of the described sound sequence
events.caption: The relief first officer took the right seat. The exact time isn’t known.

events.title: Oceanic clearance issued
events.detail: The controller issued a clearance via North Atlantic Track Zulu. The crew read it back.
events.caption: The controller cleared an Atlantic crossing route, and the crew repeated the instructions back.

events.title: Cruise level reached
events.detail: FDR and radar indicated the aircraft leveled at assigned FL330. This is a pressure flight level, not a verified geometric height.
events.caption: The aircraft leveled off at its assigned cruise level.

events.title: Last radio transmission
events.detail: The captain checked in on the new Center frequency. This was the last transmission received from the aircraft.
events.locator: s1 p.3 and footnote 8; s8 p.4
events.caption: The captain checked in on a new radio frequency. This was the aircraft’s last received transmission.

events.title: Captain announces short absence
events.detail: The captain said he would leave briefly for the toilet. Seat-motor and later door sounds followed.
events.caption: The captain announced a brief bathroom visit. Seat and door sounds followed.

events.title: Cockpit door sound
events.detail: The CVR recorded a sound similar to the cockpit door operating.
events.caption: A sound resembling the cockpit door operating was recorded.

events.title: Unidentified comment
events.detail: A three-syllable comment could not be reliably identified. The CVR group did not agree on words or language; it must not be played as a known hydraulic warning.
events.locator: s4 transcript p.35/PDF 44 (timestamp visually checked); s1 p.4 footnote 10 and p.24
events.caption: A brief comment was recorded, but its words and language remain unknown.

events.title: First translated phrase
events.detail: The relief first officer quietly spoke the phrase translated in the later quoted event. The report does not identify an aircraft anomaly before this statement.
events.caption: The relief first officer spoke quietly. No aircraft problem had been identified before this statement.

events.title: Seat motor sound
events.detail: The CVR recorded a sound similar to an electric seat motor. It does not by itself establish the occupant’s purpose.
events.caption: A sound resembling an electric seat motor was recorded. Its purpose is unknown.

events.title: Autopilot engagement signal changes
events.detail: The FDR center-autopilot discrete changed to not engaged. The final report rounds this event to 01:49:45 EST; no autopilot-disconnect warning tone was heard.
events.locator: s2 p.3 point 2; s3 printed p.71/PDF 73; s1 p.4 footnote 12
events.caption: The autopilot disengaged. No disconnect warning tone was heard.

events.title: Relief officer repeats phrase
events.detail: The official transcript translates a quietly spoken Arabic phrase as shown. Its wording alone does not establish motive or an emergency.
events.locator: s4 transcript p.36/PDF 45; s1 p.4 footnote 11
events.caption: The relief first officer repeated a quiet phrase. The words alone do not establish a motive or emergency.

events.title: Throttles move toward idle
events.detail: The final report places the manual-rate throttle movement to idle at this time. The FDR table contains earlier frame labels for the sampled lever-angle change.
events.caption: The engine power levers moved to idle.

events.title: Initial nose-down movement
events.detail: Both elevators deflected downward and the aircraft began pitching down. The initiating action is interpreted differently by NTSB and ECAA.
events.locator: s1 pp.4,37; see perspectives for causal attribution
events.caption: Both tail controls moved downward, and the aircraft began lowering its nose.

events.title: Master caution tones
events.detail: The CVR recorded four tones similar to the master-caution beeper. The transcript does not assign a unique system cause to these tones.
events.caption: Four caution tones sounded. Their specific cause is unknown.

events.title: Further downward elevator movement
events.detail: Around 01:50:05-06 EST both elevators moved farther downward. The aircraft experienced negative load factors shortly afterward.
events.locator: s1 pp.5,37; time denotes approximate start of interval
events.caption: Both tail controls moved farther downward at about this time.

events.title: Captain asks about the upset
events.detail: The captain’s voice was recorded as he returned. The final report associates this with his return to the cockpit.
events.caption: The captain’s voice was recorded as he returned to the cockpit.

events.title: Master warning begins
events.detail: A repeating high-low warning sounded through the end of the recording. Performance analysis associates the warning with exceeding the aircraft’s maximum operating Mach of 0.86.
events.caption: A warning began as the aircraft exceeded its speed limit. It continued until the recording ended.

events.title: Lowest recorded pitch sample
events.detail: The FDR summary row gives pitch -40.25 degrees. This is a frame label; individual parameter samples fall within that second.
events.locator: s3 printed p.74/PDF 76; s2 p.3 point 6
events.caption: The aircraft’s nose pointed about 40 degrees below level, its lowest recorded angle.

events.title: Elevators begin moving upward
events.detail: Both surfaces began moving back toward nose up. The subsequent reduction in descent rate was calculated from the recorded flight data.
events.caption: Both tail controls began moving to raise the nose. The descent then slowed.

events.title: Maximum descent rate estimate
events.detail: The NTSB calculated a peak descent rate of about 39,000 ft/min, at about 24,600 ft MSL. Vertical speed was not directly recorded.
events.locator: s1 p.38; published NTSB performance reconstruction
events.method: Published NTSB aircraft-performance reconstruction from FDR, radar and weather, as described in s1 Accident Sequence Study. No new path model was calculated here.
events.caption: The aircraft’s fastest descent was estimated at about 39,000 feet per minute.

events.title: Right engine fuel cutoff signal
events.detail: The right engine-start-lever discrete changed from Run to Cutoff. This records a lever state, not the identity of the person moving it.
events.locator: s2 p.4 point 10; s3 printed p.75/PDF 77
events.caption: The right engine’s fuel lever moved to cutoff. Who moved it is unknown.

events.title: Elevator split begins
events.detail: The final report places the split at about this time: left elevator nose up, right elevator nose down. The split persisted to the end of FDR data; differing causes are presented in perspectives.
events.caption: At about this time, the left tail control raised the nose while the right pushed it down.

events.title: Left engine fuel cutoff signal
events.detail: The left engine-start-lever discrete changed to Cutoff. Both engines then spooled down; the NTSB attributes the later recorder stoppage to electrical power loss after shutdown.
events.locator: s2 p.4 point 10; s3 printed p.75/PDF 77; s1 p.6 footnote 17
events.caption: The left engine’s fuel lever moved to cutoff. Both engines slowed, later cutting electrical power to the recorders.

events.title: Peak Mach estimate
events.detail: The NTSB calculated a peak Mach number of about 0.99, near 22,200 ft MSL. This is not a directly recorded Mach value.
events.locator: s1 p.38, published NTSB performance reconstruction
events.method: Published NTSB aircraft-performance reconstruction from FDR, radar and weather, as described in s1 Accident Sequence Study. No new path model was calculated here.
events.caption: The aircraft’s peak speed was estimated at nearly the speed of sound.

events.title: Throttle-angle samples rise
events.detail: The FDR sampled left/right throttle resolver angles of 84.11 and 84.99 degrees. Advancing these levers did not reverse the separate fuel-cutoff switch positions.
events.locator: s2 p.3 point 3; s3 printed p.75/PDF 77
events.caption: The engine power levers moved forward, but the separate fuel controls remained shut off.

events.title: Captain questions engine shutdown
events.detail: The captain asked whether the engines had been shut down. The engine fuel-lever states and later dialogue are recorded, but who operated every control is inferred.
events.caption: The captain asked whether the engines had been shut down.

events.title: Speedbrake handle reaches deployment
events.detail: The FDR summary row gives speedbrake-handle position 99.2%. Spoiler-panel positions were not recorded, so a handle command is not a measured panel angle.
events.locator: s2 p.5 point 13; s3 printed p.75/PDF 77; s1 p.25
events.caption: The handle for the wing’s braking panels reached nearly full deployment. The panels’ actual positions are unknown.

events.title: Strong elevator split sample
events.detail: The FDR row gives left elevator +3.87 degrees and right elevator -2.29 degrees. Positive means trailing edge up. Neither control-column force nor column position was recorded.
events.caption: The left tail control pointed upward while the right pointed downward. Pilot control movements were not recorded.

events.title: Captain calls for shared pull
events.detail: The captain asked the other pilot to pull with him. Similar calls appear at 01:50:34.78 and 01:50:36.84 EST.
events.caption: The captain repeatedly asked the other pilot to help pull back on the controls.

events.title: Last Nantucket beacon return
events.detail: The final report identifies this as the last secondary-radar return received at Nantucket. The last New York Center computer Mode C return had been at 01:50:29 EST.
events.locator: s1 p.6 and footnote 22; s8 p.4
events.caption: Nantucket received the aircraft’s last radar signal sent by its onboard transmitter.

events.title: Flight data recording ends
events.detail: The final valid FDR parameter was recorded. Its time differs from the final frame label, 01:50:35.98 EST.
events.locator: s1 pp.6,25 and footnote 17; s2 pp.2,5
events.caption: The flight recorder stopped recording flight data.

events.title: First descent stops approximately
events.detail: Radar and performance analysis indicate that the dive bottomed near 16,000 ft MSL and was followed by a climb. This is an estimate beyond FDR coverage.
events.method: Published NTSB aircraft-performance reconstruction from FDR, radar and weather, as described in s1 Accident Sequence Study. No new path model was calculated here.
events.caption: The first dive ended near an estimated 16,000 feet, followed by a climb.

events.title: Cockpit voice recording ends
events.detail: The official transcript ends at this time. It does not record ocean impact.
events.caption: The cockpit voice recording ended before the aircraft struck the ocean.

events.title: Climb ends approximately
events.detail: Primary radar and performance analysis indicate a climb to about 25,000 ft MSL, with a turn toward about 140 degrees. A second descent followed.
events.method: Published NTSB aircraft-performance reconstruction from FDR, radar and weather, as described in s1 Accident Sequence Study. No new path model was calculated here.
events.caption: The aircraft climbed to about 25,000 feet and turned before descending again.

events.title: Last New York primary return
events.detail: The ATC group report says this was the last primary target received by New York Center. Target history symbols remained displayed afterward.
events.caption: New York Center received its last radar echo. Earlier target markers remained on the display.

events.title: Estimated ocean impact
events.detail: The NTSB’s reconstruction estimates impact around this time. Only seven primary returns were available in the second descent, with potentially large altitude errors; this is not a recorded impact time.
events.method: Published NTSB aircraft-performance reconstruction from FDR, radar and weather, as described in s1 Accident Sequence Study. No new path model was calculated here.
events.caption: The aircraft struck the ocean at about this time. The exact impact time is unknown.

events.title: Controller calls after contact loss
events.detail: The controller reported radar contact lost and requested a transponder recycle. There was no response.
events.caption: The controller reported lost radar contact and requested a reset of the aircraft’s radar transmitter. No response came.

events.title: Rescue authorities notified
events.detail: The area manager notified the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center and Coast Guard. No seconds are supplied in the source.
events.caption: The area manager notified Air Force and Coast Guard rescue authorities.

events.title: Flight data recorder recovered
events.detail: The US Navy recovered the FDR on 9 November 1999. It was kept wet and transported to the NTSB laboratory; recovery time of day was not established.
events.caption: The Navy recovered the flight recorder on November 9, 1999, and sent it to investigators.

events.title: Egyptian report records unresolved cause
events.detail: In June 2001, ECAA said no single causal sequence was established and called an elevator defect plausible and likely. It rejected an intentional-crash interpretation.
events.caption: Egyptian investigators left the cause unresolved, considered a tail control defect likely, and rejected an intentional crash.

events.title: NTSB adopts probable cause
events.detail: On 13 March 2002, the NTSB adopted its finding that the relief first officer’s flight-control inputs caused departure from cruise and impact. It did not determine the reason for those actions.
events.locator: s1 cover and p.67; time of day not specified
events.caption: U.S. investigators attributed the crash to the relief first officer’s control movements. His reason remains unknown.

perspectives.label: NTSB control inputs
perspectives.held_by: US National Transportation Safety Board; Boeing’s technical submission also rejected a mechanical cause.
perspectives.claim: The NTSB found that the relief first officer’s flight-control inputs caused the departure from cruise and subsequent impact. It inferred opposing pilot inputs during the elevator split and attributed engine shutdown to the relief first officer. The reason for his actions was not determined; a specific suicide or revenge motive is not an established finding.

evidence_for.text: FDR surface movements and CVR sequence: no identified anomaly before autopilot disconnect; downward elevator inputs preceded the captain’s return; upward movement began afterward. The late split and each surface’s relation to load-factor changes were consistent with two functioning elevators. s1 pp.52-67.

The NTSB evaluated cable and actuator failures. Tested failures did not match the full recorded elevator-motion sequence; a cable break/jam could match only the first few seconds. Simulated recovery remained possible from either pilot column. s1 pp.52-57.

Initial upset took place below Mach 0.91, within the validated data range. NTSB estimated that matching initial elevator displacement with the proposed failures would require a hinge-moment error of about 79%. s1 p.56 footnote 99.

evidence_against.text: Control-column positions and forces were not recorded. Attribution of specific actions to each pilot is inferred from surface motion, cockpit layout and voice/sound timing, not directly measured. s1 p.25.

ECAA disputed simulator fidelity, steady-state force assumptions, interpretation of damaged actuator parts and aerodynamic extrapolation above Mach 0.91. The NTSB acknowledged transonic uncertainty but found it insufficient to overturn its analysis. s1 pp.47-51,56-57; s6 sections 2.3 and 3.2.

The NTSB found no conclusive explanation for the relief first officer’s actions. ECAA argued that the dialogue showed cooperation and that the religious phrase was an ordinary request for assistance, not proof of suicidal intent.

ending.description: NTSB inferred opposed elevator commands while the captain tried to recover. After the recorders stopped, radar indicated a climb and another descent. Do not animate a proved struggle, a known motive, or exact final cockpit actions.

perspectives.label: ECAA elevator failure hypothesis
perspectives.held_by: Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority investigation team, with EgyptAir technical submissions.
perspectives.claim: ECAA said the evidence could not establish one causal sequence and regarded an elevator-system defect as plausible and likely. Its main scenario involved a latent right-elevator actuator fault followed by another actuator jam, with pilot recovery efforts and possible later elevator loss. It called for further investigation rather than proving a particular failed component.

evidence_for.text: Recovered elevator bellcrank rivets were sheared; one actuator had a sheared pin and displaced bias spring. ECAA considered aspects of the damage inconsistent with water impact. Fleet bellcrank failures and related FAA directives showed a real safety issue. s6 sections 1.17,2.3,3.1; s1 pp.18-19,34-35.

ECAA argued that elevator offsets after autopilot disconnect could reflect a latent right-side actuator fault, and that dynamic cable/override behaviour could differ from Boeing’s simpler force assumptions. Its addendum disputed interpretation of subsequent ground tests.

ECAA argued that the aileron behaviour and limited validated transonic data made precise high-speed elevator/column inferences unsafe. It proposed partial or complete loss of the right elevator as an explanation for later performance.

evidence_against.text: The NTSB found no scraping or abrasion indicating a jam at the displaced spring, and could not establish that the pin/spring conditions preceded impact. Sheared bellcrank rivets alone do not prove an in-flight initiating failure. s1 pp.34-35.

The NTSB found that both surfaces initially moved upward together and that the right elevator later exceeded the deflections possible in tested failed-actuator scenarios. Simulations found recovery possible despite the hypothesised faults. s1 pp.55-57.

Only about 37% of elevator surface area and four of six elevator actuators were recovered. Missing and impact-damaged evidence prevents proving the proposed precise failure chain. NTSB aerodynamic/load-factor analysis did not support loss of the right elevator during the recorded split. s1 pp.34-35,63-64.

ending.description: ECAA interprets the crew as attempting to recover from a mechanical upset and proposes possible right-elevator damage or loss during the dive. It did not establish a separate timestamped geographic route. No track override is supplied because none was recovered as numeric data.

perspectives.label: Possible traffic avoidance
perspectives.held_by: ECAA and EgyptAir as an unresolved alternative, not a demonstrated occurrence.
perspectives.claim: ECAA retained the possibility that the relief first officer manoeuvred to avoid a perceived collision or another emergency. It questioned unidentified radar returns and incomplete access to radar evaluation data. It did not establish an intruding aircraft, missile or collision.

evidence_for.text: ECAA linked some primary returns into apparent tracks crossing Flight 990’s path and requested additional radar information. s6 sections 2.4,3.1-3.2.

The NTSB radar addendum confirms that controlled Air Force baseline-evaluation documents were not released to ECAA. Lack of that access is a real limitation, although it is not evidence of an external object.

evidence_against.text: NTSB found no intersecting aircraft or projectile trajectory in four of five radar records. The anomalous returns appeared at Riverhead without matching returns in overlapping coverage. s1 p.36.

84 RADES attributed the returns to radio-frequency interference from Bucks Harbor. FAA supplied identical frequency pairs for Bucks Harbor and Riverhead; the Air Force reported most interference disappeared after a frequency change. s9 pp.2-3.
No corroborated crossing object or physical evidence of foreign-object impact, explosion or fire was found. Those results weigh against a physical external-threat explanation. s1 pp.35-36,52.

ending.description: This hypothesis changes the proposed reason for the initial manoeuvre, not any established ending location. No measured conflicting-aircraft position or alternative Flight 990 trajectory is available for an override.

evidence_points.label: Eastern debris field
evidence_points.detail: Approximate sonar-mapped center; about 83 by 73 m. Contained most fuselage, wings, empennage, right engine, main gear and recorders. This is a seabed accumulation, not an exact impact point. s1 p.34.

evidence_points.label: Western debris field
evidence_points.detail: Approximate center; about 62 by 66 m. Mainly left-engine parts with smaller structural pieces and most of the nose landing gear. Centers about 366 m apart. s1 p.34.

evidence_points.label: ATC last-position reference
evidence_points.detail: Rounded position used as a marker in meteorology radar images. s5 p.4 gives this as the ATC last known position but does not give the target timestamp; do not add it to the timed track as if exact.

witnesses.who: Nearby Air France flight crew during the search
witnesses.said: Paraphrase: after being vectored over the last known position, the crew reported overcast conditions with some view below and saw nothing unusual. This was a later search overflight, not an eyewitness account of the crash. s8 p.5; coordination began at 07:31:50 UTC.

why_it_matters: The investigation examined a real 767 elevator bellcrank shear-rivet problem; FAA directives required functional checks and then recurring elevator-system testing, without establishing that this defect caused Flight 990. The case also supported NTSB recommendations for cockpit image recorders to resolve gaps about control actions. Sources: s1 pp.18-19 and p.61 footnote 109; s6 section 1.17.

conflicts.a: NTSB: the relief first officer’s control inputs caused the descent and impact; reason undetermined.
conflicts.b: ECAA: a unique causal sequence cannot be established; mechanical defect is plausible and likely, and intentional crashing is unsupported.

conflicts.a: NTSB: functioning elevators responded to opposed pilot-column inputs.
conflicts.b: ECAA: actuator faults, dynamic override behaviour and possible right-elevator loss undermine that interpretation.

conflicts.a: NTSB found impact damage, no jam-witness marks on the displaced spring, and no demonstrated initiating failure.
conflicts.b: ECAA considered some failure patterns inconsistent with impact and evidence warranting further mechanical study.

conflicts.a: NTSB accepted extrapolation above Mach 0.91, while acknowledging uncertainty; the initial upset occurred within the validated range.
conflicts.b: ECAA argued that transonic aerodynamics, simulator and force-model limitations prevented ruling out its failure scenarios.

conflicts.a: NTSB/84 RADES attributed Riverhead anomalies to interference; other overlapping radars did not corroborate a crossing object.
conflicts.b: ECAA linked apparent tracks and said withheld baseline data prevented a full independent check. The withholding is documented in the NTSB addendum.

conflicts.about: Last secondary return: different data streams
conflicts.a: ZNY computer extraction: final Mode C return at 06:50:29 UTC, FL183.
conflicts.b: Final report: last return received at Nantucket at 06:50:34 UTC. These are different receiver/processing endpoints, not two interchangeable aircraft-loss times.

conflicts.a: Early factual summaries in FDR/weather reports say about 01:22 EST.
conflicts.b: Final report says about 01:20 EST; FDR air/ground transition is 01:20:45.98 EST. Use the recorded transition for chronology, not the early approximate summary.

conflicts.a: FDR factual report gives last frame label 01:50:35.98 EST; raw summary rows use that frame clock.
conflicts.b: Final report gives last actual parameter 01:50:36.64 EST and rounds many actions to the following whole second. Do not shift every parameter by an invented universal offset.

conflicts.a: Some CVR group members thought the 01:48:30 EST syllables resembled English words about control or hydraulics.
conflicts.b: There was no agreement; the official group rendered the comment unintelligible. Neither interpretation is an established quote.

conflicts.a: Docket item title labels the addendum November 2, 2002.
conflicts.b: The opened document cover says November 2, 2001. The internal document date is used here.

unknowns: Exact motive or reason for the relief first officer’s actions. NTSB did not determine it; neither a specific suicide motive nor a revenge story is established by the finding.

Continuous geographic flight path. No timestamped latitude/longitude table was recovered. The opened raw-data manifest links to local files that are not embedded, and the current main performance-study PDF download returned an empty body. Track coordinates are null; no great-circle, dead-reckoned or chart-digitized positions were invented.

Raw pressure altitude is not corrected geometric or local barometric MSL height. The added pressure_alt_ft field preserves the recorder values; alt_ft remains null for those rows. Only published NTSB approximate MSL reconstruction anchors populate alt_ft. A dense MSL altitude conversion was not recovered.

The raw airspeed channel is labelled computed airspeed. It is preserved as computed_airspeed_kt; an exact IAS-channel interpretation was not established, so ias_kt remains null. Mach was calculated by investigators, not recorded. Groundspeed samples were not recovered.
The FDR vane-angle column is not a calibrated aircraft body angle of attack. Its raw negative cruise values are preserved as vane_aoa_deg, while aoa_deg is null. No offset was guessed.

Heading from FDR is magnetic. No event-date declination conversion to true heading was performed. The published post-recorder 140-degree heading has an unspecified reference and is only an approximate reconstruction anchor.

Precise subsecond sampling offsets for every FDR channel were not applied. Each selected row uses the official frame label; the channels are not simultaneous measurements at that exact instant. Left/right elevator sampling offsets must be respected in a higher-resolution animation.

The control columns, wheels, pilot forces and spoiler-panel positions were not recorded. The FDR sampled elevator surfaces and speedbrake-handle command; individual pilot actions and panel geometry cannot all be directly observed.

Exact flap and landing-gear positions at every selected timestamp were not extracted from the corresponding slower recorded channels. These fields remain null; cruise configuration was not silently filled into every frame.

Exact flight path, height, attitude, control inputs and breakup time after recorder stoppage. Seven primary returns during the second descent have potentially large altitude errors. The estimated 06:52:30 UTC impact time is not an instrument log of water contact.

Exact water-entry point and aircraft orientation. Seabed debris-field centers are known approximately but must not be treated as a precise impact trajectory or proof of the time an engine or elevator separated.
Which damaged elevator parts, if any, failed before impact. Not all actuators and elevator surfaces were recovered; NTSB and ECAA disagree about damage interpretation.

Historical coordinates of DOVEY and complete numeric 1999 planned route were not verified. The route shown is the accident JFK-Cairo leg; the same service had earlier departed Los Angeles. Current airport reference coordinates are contextual, not 1999 runway endpoints.
Exact same-day livery: a verified photograph eleven days before the accident was opened and viewed, but no photograph taken on 31 October was established.

A single aircraft-specific overall height and a primary-source wing-sweep number were not established. Boeing’s ground-height range depends on load and attitude; height_m and wing_sweep_deg remain null. Fuselage_diameter_m uses sourced external width, not an assertion of a circular cross-section.

Accident-site cloud base, exact cloud coverage, visibility through cloud, turbulence, lightning, sea state and wave height. Remote METARs, a six-hour-old sounding and satellite cloud-top estimates do not determine all local layers. No wave or sea-state measurement was located in the opened meteorology record.
Time of day for FDR recovery and investigation/report milestones. Events with day/month evidence but no clock time use t_utc=null and state the date in detail.

sources.notes: Downloaded with curl and extracted with pypdf. 160 PDF pages including attachments. Adopted 13 March 2002; corrected 27 March 2002. sources.title: FDR Attachment 3: EgyptAir Flight 990 FDR Tabular Data Sets
sources.notes: 164 PDF pages. Summary-data tables, printed 24 April 2000, occupy PDF pages 3-78, printed pages 1-76. All 756 summary rows were extracted and 130 selected without interpolation. sources.notes: 47 PDF pages, dated 10 February 2000 (cover visually checked). sources.title: Meteorology Group Factual Report
sources.notes: Six pages, dated 20 December 1999, read throughout; METAR and sounding tables also checked as rendered pages. Section D gives UTC directly, true wind direction, MSL upper-air heights, and AGL METAR cloud bases. Astronomical values are US Naval Observatory calculations for the upset at 33,000 feet. The cloud-top estimate is satellite/sounding analysis, not a direct cloud-height measurement at the aircraft.

sources.title: Report of Investigation of Accident: EgyptAir Flight 990
sources.notes: 223 PDF pages including appendices; June 2001. Printed pages 139-142 (PDF 147-150) give findings and probable-cause discussion. Sections 2.3, 2.4 and appendices develop the elevator and radar objections. ECAA explicitly says evidence is insufficient to identify a single causal sequence; it regards an elevator defect as plausible and likely. This must not be recast as a proven elevator failure.

sources.title: Addendum 1 to the ECAA Report of Investigation
sources.notes: 38 pages. The docket title says November 2, 2002, but the document cover actually says November 2, 2001. The cover date is used here. Read its background, ground-test descriptions and conclusions about cable break/jam and high-breakout-force pogo tests. These are ECAA interpretations of tests, not established failures on SU-GAP.

sources.title: Air Traffic Control Group Chairman Factual Report
sources.notes: 10 PDF pages opened; the chronology and display-filtering discussion were read. Pages 3-5 provide UTC chronology, Mode C returns and controller-display filtering. The last New York Center Mode C return at 06:50:29 differs from the later last Nantucket return discussed in the final report; these concern different radar records. Controller display XXXX did not mean the raw altitude data were absent.

sources.title: Aircraft Performance Addendum 3: Radar Interference Information
sources.notes: Three pages, dated 2 August 2000, read throughout. John O’Callaghan documents the ECAA request, refusal to release controlled baseline evaluations, matching Riverhead/Bucks Harbor frequencies, and an Air Force report that interference mostly disappeared after a temporary frequency change on 15 May 2000.
